_note: SAMPLE. Generated from the hypothesised draft so the pages can be built and reviewed before Thursday. Replaced by live data on draft day.

roast.text: Two days after Bijan Robinson set the running back contract record, Gibbs signed a bigger one. Jesse spent the 1.01 on a man whose defining recent act was waiting for someone else to name a price and then beating it. Fitting, since nobody was going to take him first but Jesse anyway.

Josh Allen at three, best player on the board, superflex, no argument available. Keshia did the correct thing at the correct moment, which we are choosing to read as a clerical event rather than a decision. The rest of America was letting him slide to 19.

Three of the picks before this one were running backs, so Jay looked at the board and took the running back. Jonathan Taylor at six, national ADP 6.33. Not a pick so much as a mild compliance exercise.

Amon-Ra St. Brown, best available, and Justin actually got him a little later than the country does at 8.35. There is no reach here, no imbalance, nothing to work with. Somebody check whether his mouse slipped onto the right name.
James Cook III was there. So were De'Von Achane and Drake Maye. Mike took Hurts six slots ahead of where the board had him, in a format where the QB would still have been there a while.
Cook was the best player left and Evan took the best player left, one slot after the board said to. Bold. The kind of pick that gets made by a team still labeled Waiting to draft.

For Jefferson at 18 to look smart, Kenneth Walker III has to disappoint, Breece Hall has to disappoint, and Matthew Stafford has to be irrelevant in a two-quarterback league. Three separate things, all outside Tyler's control. Also that is his second receiver and zero quarterbacks.
Thirty better players were on the board and Bree took Chris Olave. Breece Hall, ranked 19th, was one of them. The rest of America had Olave going 29th and even that was generous relative to this.

Etienne at 24 needs Ashton Jeanty to bust, Jeremiyah Love to bust, and CeeDee Lamb to have been overrated by everyone. Fourteen better players remained. Jesse passed on all of them to take a back thirteen slots early.

Collins is expected to lead the Texans receiving corps after Jayden Higgins tore his ACL, which is the most encouraging sentence available and still does not cover twenty slots. CeeDee Lamb was sitting there at 24. Chenell paid for the target share and skipped the actual star.

Two quarterbacks came off the board in the previous handful of picks, so Evan reached for the most famous one left, four slots after the board said he was fair game. Best available, listed questionable, zero imagination required. The rest of America takes Mahomes at 108, which is the only interesting thing about pick 36.

Four quarterbacks. That is the entire roster. Mike has not drafted a running back, a receiver or a tight end, and Jaxson Dart, whose Giants trio with Skattebo and Nabers played 18 snaps together in 2025 and who analysts kept flagging as overvalued into 2026, is the fourth one.

Justin Herbert, ranked 38th, was sitting right there in a two-quarterback format. Drake London and Caleb Williams too. Colin took McMillan 18 slots early instead, which is 18 different ways to feel bad about it later.

Goff at 51 is the best player on the board, seven slots after he could have been taken, and the country does not touch him until 136. That is a genuinely sound piece of value work from Keshia. Then you notice it is her fourth quarterback and one running back, and the whole thing starts to look like a coincidence.

For this to pay off, Jordan Love has to be a nonfactor in a superflex league, Garrett Wilson has to fade, and George Pickens has to have been a mirage. That is 29 better players Tyler needs to be wrong about at once. DJ Moore was rated 84th and got picked 55th, which is a lot of faith to spread around.

Fannin is the second Brown Justin has pulled in the same neighbourhood, eleven slots ahead of where the board had him. George Pickens was still there at 56. Nothing says roster construction like buying the same offence twice and calling it a tight end.

Nobody in the country is taking Tony Pollard at 65 -- the national number is 90.74, and the league board agrees at 90. Colin got there 25 slots early anyway, stepping over Zay Flowers, DeVonta Smith and George Kittle to do it. Fourth running back, and the only quarterback is still the one.

George Kittle, 63rd on the board, went untouched so that Bree could take a quarterback ranked 79th. Bucky Irving too. Darnold is her second quarterback in a format that starts two, which is the single sentence keeping this pick out of court.

Five running backs. One receiver. One quarterback in superflex. Tuten is the best player available and seven slots of value, and Doug still managed to make it the least useful correct pick of the round.

Metcalf works if Sam LaPorta stays a backup-quality tight end, Rome Odunze never breaks out, and Tee Higgins was overrated by 21 spots' worth of consensus. Chenell needs all of that, plus a receiver listed questionable to be fine. The board had him 97th and she called his number at 76.

Two quarterbacks, five receivers, zero running backs. Tyler has built half a fantasy team and the half he skipped is the one where you have to start people. Rome Odunze at 70 was there, and would also have been a receiver, which at this point is apparently the only requirement.

Burden suffered a groin injury on 8 August in a contested red-zone rep. James read that and moved him up 11 slots past Rome Odunze and Tee Higgins, which is one interpretation of the news. That is his third receiver and second in five picks, so at least the pattern is consistent.

Odunze was the best player left, ranked 70th, and Justin got him at 82 with nobody better on the board. No reach, no passed-over stud, no jersey loyalty, nothing to work with. Somebody check whether he meant to click the name above it.

Tee Higgins was the highest-ranked man alive at 83 and the third receiver taken in five picks, so Mike joined the queue and took the obvious one. The country had him at 51, so nobody will ever question it. Five quarterbacks, one running back, and this was the moment he decided to play it safe.

Eight rounds in, Evan has one quarterback in a format that starts two, and he spent this pick on a back who was out-touched by TreVeyon Henderson 25.1% to 18.9% last season. Stevenson was the best player available at 74, which is true and also not the point. The point is the empty second quarterback slot that has been empty since round one.

McLaurin, 76th on the board, taken at 86 with nobody better remaining and the rest of America paying 61 for him. That is the fourth receiver in five picks and Mike's second straight piece of actual value. Two correct picks in a row from a man holding five quarterbacks feels less like a plan and more like the board ran out of ways to trick him.

Henderson held a 25.1% touch share to Stevenson's 18.9% last season, and James has drafted that number as though it is a workload. It is a New England committee, and committees do not care what happened before. Third running back, still one quarterback.

Round eight, and the quarterback count at 4th and Inshes remains one. Colin's answer was a second tight end, 37 slots ahead of the national number, which is a lovely bit of shopping in a league that will start exactly one of them. Two tight ends, three running backs, and one man expected to play both quarterback slots at once.

Dowdle was the best player left and Bree paid roughly what the country pays, which is the correct thing to do. Then you look up and see three tight ends, one running back and one quarterback in superflex. The pick is fine; everything surrounding it is a crime scene.

Warren joins a roster that now runs four deep at running back, and Chenell has been assembling this backfield like she is buying the whole depth chart rather than a starter. Nine picks in and there is still no quarterback anywhere on it. Great value at 93, wrong shop.

Six running backs. One receiver. Dobbins was genuinely the best name left at 98 and the country pays 112 for him, so the price is not the issue; the issue is that Doug's starting lineup is now a running back convention with a single guest speaker at wideout.

Kyle Monangai averaged 6.9 touches a game last season and is pushing D'Andre Swift for Chicago's backfield, which Bree has decided is worth 23 slots ahead of the national price. Fair enough on the value. Less fair is the three tight ends and one quarterback sitting behind him in superflex.

Two quarterback slots, one quarterback, and Jay's answer in round nine was a fourth receiver three spots ahead of the board with Isaiah Likely still sitting there at 102. America was paying 79 for Harrison, which is the only part of this anybody can defend. The empty slot does not care how good the receiver is.

Likely at 104, two slots after the board wanted him, 19 ahead of the national number, nobody better left. Colin has been assembling tight ends all afternoon and this is the one time the habit accidentally produced correct behaviour. Fourth tight end, one quarterback, and somehow a good pick.

Twenty-six better players were on the board and James went 26 slots early for a Cardinals receiver, which is a strange amount of enthusiasm for one NFL depth chart. Christian Watson, Hunter Henry and T.J. Hockenson all sat there watching. The jersey may be nice; the roster is not.

Round nine closes with Evan taking a tight end 41 slots ahead of the national price, which is a lovely bit of value in a lineup that will start one of them and cannot start a second quarterback because he does not own one. Two tight ends, three receivers, three backs, and a hole at the position the format doubled. Hockenson was the best man left, which is the softest possible cushion for a very hard problem.

Five receivers, three backs, one tight end, one quarterback. Golden came in at exactly the national price with nobody better available, so this is a clean pick attached to the ugliest roster shape in the room. James is building a wide receiver corps for a league that asks him to start two quarterbacks.

Another Chief for Jay, ten slots ahead of the board, and the collection now looks less like a roster than a season-ticket photo. Aaron Jones Sr., Michael Pittman Jr. and Josh Jacobs were all left behind so this could happen. Sixth receiver, three backs, one quarterback.

Aaron Jones Sr. at 116, five slots after the board had him, within half a pick of the national price, best player left. Nothing to grab onto at all. Bree has three tight ends and one quarterback in superflex, so we can only conclude the mouse slipped somewhere useful.

Pittman goes to Chenell at 117, listed questionable, 27 slots later than the country was paying, with nobody better on the board. Fourth receiver, fourth running back, one quarterback. She keeps buying insurance on positions she has already over-covered and none on the one the format doubled.

Eighteen better players were sitting there, and one of them was Josh Jacobs, who lasted exactly one more pick. Doug went 18 slots early on Diggs anyway, and Mike Evans was also just sitting in the pile. Six running backs, two receivers, and the receiver he finally reached for cost him the best back left.

Three quarterbacks. Five running backs. Two receivers. Jesse got the best player on the board at a 60-slot discount to the national price and still walked away with a lineup that looks like it was assembled by two different people who never spoke.

That is Doug's seventh running back and his second in five picks, which at this point is less a backfield than a waiting room. Kenny Gainwell and Brenton Strange were both there. Nine better players existed and he took the seventh guy at the position he already has too many of.

Best player left, 21 slots after the country was paying, and none of that changes the number that matters: one quarterback. Round eleven, five running backs, four receivers, a tight end, and a single arm in a format that starts two. Chenell keeps winning the pick and losing the roster.

Croskey-Merritt at 125, five slots after the board wanted him, eleven ahead of the national number, nobody better available. Bree stumbled into the correct answer during a run at the position, which is the draft equivalent of finding your keys in the fridge. Three tight ends and one quarterback suggest the process has not changed.

The country was paying 170 for Evan Engram. Jay paid 126, which is 44 slots of enthusiasm nobody else in America was offering, with Terrance Ferguson and Brian Thomas Jr. both still there. Thirty-one better players, second tight end, one quarterback.

MarShawn Lloyd at 129 with 24 better players on the board, among them Brian Thomas Jr., who went one pick into the next round and will be someone else's flex all year. Jakobi Meyers and Aaron Rodgers also declined to disappear. Third back in five picks for a man with one quarterback.

Justin adds a fifth receiver to two running backs and calls it a roster. Thomas was the best man available and seven slots later than the board wanted him, which is fine work, but the shape underneath it is a rumour. Two backs in round eleven is not a hedge, it is a dare.

Six receivers now, and still one quarterback, in the format that asks for two every single week. The Addison pick itself is unimpeachable: best player left, three slots after the board, 16 cheaper than the national price. James has spent twelve rounds solving a problem the league does not have.

Jeudy was going 168 in the rest of the country. Colin took him at 137, 26 slots ahead of the board, with Quentin Johnston, Cam Ward and Khalil Shakir all still on it. Nobody else on earth makes this pick here, which Colin will insist is the point.
One running back. Six receivers. Three tight ends. Tyler has assembled a roster that can catch anything and carry nothing, and Wan'Dale Robinson is the third receiver he has taken in five picks.

Quentin Johnston sat at 134 and Jay went to 165 for Calvin Ridley instead, 26 slots ahead of where the board had him with 26 better players behind him. Cam Ward was also right there, which matters, because this is a sixth receiver joining one quarterback.

Shakir is the fourth receiver taken in five picks and the best player left, six slots after the board wanted him. The problem is what he joins: five quarterbacks, three tight ends and now two receivers, a roster built entirely out of the positions you can only start one or two of.

Jalen Nailor was going 171 in the rest of the country. Doug paid 143, with Gunnar Helm, De'Zhaun Stribling and Chig Okonkwo among the 29 better players he stepped around to get there. Seven running backs and three receivers is the roster this was meant to fix.

Thirteen rounds, four running backs, six receivers, and the tight end count just went to two. The arm count did not move. Chris Godwin Jr. was one of 22 better players on the board, and James took a tight end 22 slots early to avoid the one position the format demands twice.

Three tight ends, three running backs, and Deebo Samuel Sr. makes five receivers. Evan took the best man left seven slots after the board asked and 14 cheaper than the country, which is fine, but this roster is now two full positions deep in players who mostly sit on the bench.

Round fourteen, and the fifth running back arrives on a roster that has six receivers and a single quarterback. Josh Downs and David Njoku were the only two men rated above Woody Marks here, so the pick is defensible. The 14 rounds spent not addressing a starting slot are not.

Four running backs, five receivers, four tight ends, one quarterback. Bree has drafted a lineup with more tight ends than the league can start twice over and Jalen Coker was genuinely the best name left, which is the tragedy of it.

Seven running backs and now six receivers, and Doug has still not drafted a tight end. Jalen McMillan was the best player available two slots after the board and five ahead of the country, so this is a fine pick sitting on a roster with a hole where a whole position should be.

Bateman is the fourth receiver in five picks and the sixth overall, joining four running backs, four tight ends, and one quarterback in a format with two starting slots for the last of those. Fifteen rounds. The board agreed with the pick, which somehow makes it worse.
